decision.audit_notes: Verified current-session dialogue; decision evidence remapped to cleaned source.

evidence.text: So here’s the thing. I’m going to pass, but this is what I have to say. I really like you and I love your ambitions. I have rarely seen an entrepreneur come in and say on 25 cents I can get to the moon. And you’re doing it. And good on you. And I love it. umm I’m going to pass But I really like you and I think you’re fixing an interesting problem.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Hello.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: So hello everyone. I’m Rahul. So I’ll take you back a few years. 26 years old. I’ve spent my whole life working in what I call an engineering outfit. Blue shirt, baggy suit, white shirt once in a while. I worked all over the midwest. I used to work for Rolls Royce, Jet Engines And then I got a job for McKinsey. So I moved to New York City, and immediately it was very apparent that whether it was serving a client or going out trying to get a date, frankly, something just didn’t work.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: And so now fast forward four weeks into New York, I’ve got a date with this girl that I’ve had a massive crush on all through college years. And I’ve got to go and pick out an outfit So then I went, I tried to shop around, six hours in, I couldn’t find anything. Tried Trunk Club. They sold me good stuff. I remember, two shirts and a pair of pants and it cost me $500. Expensive. I wore it, I looked good, I admit. But, that’s ridiculous.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: If I have a thousand dollars, 2000, 3000 to burn, anyone can make me look like James Bond. But that’s not what I have I can’t afford to do that living in New York And that’s when I realized something’s broken in the market I like to look good. I don’t know how to do it So, how do we fix that. That’s when I invented Hyde. it’s rental clothing. Like clockwork, week on week, you get your entire outfit.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: So it’s like Rent the Runway Work but for men?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: But for men. But it’s complete. Men don’t like putting together outfits. That’s what people have missed We say, no, no. What have you got going on Charles? You’ve got to go to a work dinner? Tell me where it is. Oh, you know, it’s a nice four star restaurant here. Great. I’ll put together a nice blazer for you, with dark wash jeans, with a pair of nice boots, perhaps, or wing tip shoes. All of this shows up at your doorstep. Sunglasses, cologne, everything. And you’re wearing $1500 worth of stuff for $50 so it’s easy on the wallet too.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So it’s a male Rent the Runway kind of per event ...

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: If you take Rent the Runway and merge it with Trunk Club, you get this.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: $50 a week?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: $50 per outfit.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: So I’ll walk you through the plans we have $50 for a one off. One off is basically hey, you’ve got somewhere to go, here’s your box. Thanks very much. A lot of people come back. $80 if you want it twice a month. And the last one is 150 a month, which is like clockwork every week

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: The $80 offering, is that a week’s worth of clothing? Or is that...

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: So it’s a full week’s worth of clothing?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: So it’s always two shirts, pair of pants, outerwear, shoes, belt, sunglasses, and/or a tie. And cologne and all that.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So it’s not really a week.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: It’s not a week. It’s two outfits.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: We try to optimize for an outfit and a half

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Can you show us?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Yeah, absolutely. Please go ahead.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Do you want to hand us one? Do you want to show it? What’s easier?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: There you are.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: It’s everything!

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: It’s everything

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So everything’s used?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Yes. So I wanted to put these shoes in specifically to show you.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: The shoes are quite worn, though. That kind of freaked me out a little bit.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: I put that in specifically for that reason.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I know because you have one more turn. But I’m still a little scared of that. The rest of it I could deal with.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: I wanted to show you the last turn.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay. I think we get the idea of the product.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Tell us about your sales thus far

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Ah, yes. Sales. So we now have 35 running clients. I started it in December purely sort of promotional activities. Signed with 700 people within about three weeks, give or take. We did a couple of popups. And we signed and we started supplying to 35 people. umm

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: What happened to the 700?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: That’s just our sort of active engaged user list. I can’t let in more right now without hiring more operations people. Because my product experience will fall.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Well what’s involved with that? Why is that holding you back?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: The first is the actual styling. So I want stylists to be building these boxes, not someone just randomly doing it So what I’ve built now is that stylists can assemble boxes remotely. They don’t need to be with the clothes Second component is the actual packing, the logistics of it I still need someone to actually package the boxes. Bringing everything into inventory and then checking it out of inventory, that needs to be immaculate. Right now, we don’t have things like barcode scanners so we’re all doing it manually. It works really well, but it takes time, and I need people to do that.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Can you explain the styling and the inventory? It seems like that becomes a real stumbling point.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: That’s absolutely my favorite question. So that’s the secret sauce here. What we’ve found is that four social events cover 80 to 90% of an average man’s calendar during a given week. Sunday brunch, Thursday happy hour, Friday formal date, Saturday casual date. That’s it. If I can solve for these four events for the sizes, which also by the way, living in a metropolitan city, if you look them up they cluster, the median is a 40R. If you can pick up your sizes at that median, and forget about the two tails, I can cover most of my inventory. And I’m seeing that now in my data.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Wow

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But there are a lot of different size combinations. You have all different size shoes and then different sized blazers and shirts. I’m just wondering, how many times you can turn that.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And how you can automate that a bit, too.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: So the model does exactly that right now. When you join on, it spits out to me and says, let’s say, I’m assuming you’re a 42R?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Um, yeah.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Okay. So if...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: No 42 long.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Okay. 42 long. So you come on. It’ll tell me we have three 42 long blazers for him. We are okay for three weeks. It’s predictive buying. Then it tells me for the fourth week, if he sticks on, we need to buy something for him. And so I can now time the market. I can look out for sales. I can tell my buyers to say you’ve got three weeks. If he stays on, buy him something.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Have you raised money to date?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Yeah. So we did. So we did a small round I’ve raised 100 grand from a strategic. And then $20,000 friends and family. Personally, I’ve put in about 20 grand with my partner.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So how much money are you looking for?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: A convertible note, 100 grand would be great.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: You’re looking for 100 grand?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: M-hm.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Why so little?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: I think that’ll take me to the 2500 customers I need and then we can raise a round after that. uhh I think anything greater than that at his stage will be too dilutive…

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: What’s your convertible note terms? Tell me about it.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: A $1 million cap.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Oh that’s why.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: I don’t want to give it a ridiculous valuation and... Look, I’ve done a lot of things in my professional life, I haven’t raised money.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So what’s your revenue? If you sign on those 2500 clients, what’s the revenue?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: So 2500 clients, what we’ve averaged out, what we’ve seen so far is about $100 per client a month.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And then what’s your acquisition cost?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: My acquisition cost ranged between 20 and 40 dollars. We have not done any social media marketing. I haven’t spent a single penny because I don’t know enough about it, and I know enough about it to know it’s a money hole. So I haven’t put any money on it So things we have done is I’ve gone and done fireside chats at WeWorks in DC. I’ve had popup stores at Union Market, at you know the DC startup week, etc. That’s where I’ve gotten people to sign up for the list. Then off of that list, I’ve converted people by literally going down and seeing who’s opening our emails the most we’ll only email them. That’s how we got to the 35, because I knew they would sign on.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: The only thing I would say on the marketing is a business like this is going to ultimately come down to how good you are at marketing. I mean, this is a customer acquisition business, right? umm And I don’t know if you’re planning to bring someone in ...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Or outsource it. Ideally it should be someone on your team.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Oh it has to be.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: At a senior level.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: 100%. It has to be because I want the marketing person to be fully tied in with the product development and the product roadmap. Otherwise you’re distributing different messages. So I definitely don’t want to outsource this. I just need a good person to come join. Perfectly honest about it. I know that’s a gap I need to fill very quickly.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: First off, I really like you. I’d say in a nice way you’re overly honest and straight up and I think realistic about your valuations and stuff. It’s nice. I think you’re offering a very interesting service. This is kind of cool. umm I guess what I’m struggling with is just the simple idea, is this really going to be a big business?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Fair enough. Okay. So I want to grow with the 100 grand to 2500 customers at the end of the year.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So estimated monthly revenue would be?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: We’d be at $250,000. That’s a $3 million a year business at the end of the year. Right?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Would you have a net margin at that point?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: I’ll be breaking even at 2500 customers. Now after that, it’s on the upting

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So talk about the buyers. And talk about how you... You’re raising 100,000, which sounds very, very tiny and I understand why. But it doesn’t, I can’t imagine how that 100,000 is going to actually get you to the 2500 if in fact you’re buying, you also have to pay stylists, So can you…

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: I can answer that actually. Because I ran the math on that

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: So 2500 customers, $10 a customer spending 25 grand on it. That’s 25% of the $100,000, right?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: I want about 50 grand to set up a team. I can pay them part-time. Operations and stylists.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: [laughs]

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Because I’ve got... See the thing is, stylists are not actually in the store. They can work offline. That’s the beauty of it. So if I can get that set up, they’re only putting in the hours. They’re not driving anywhere. I can have them in Minneapolis for all I care.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay but if...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And then, and what... Finish the... I mean, it just, and then what about inventory?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Okay. And inventory is actually, because we’re a cash generative business, I’m not actually putting any more money in inventory anymore. The money that the business generates, I buy new clothes with. It’s a cash generative business.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But to get started with 2500 people, you got to buy inventory.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: I won’t go zero to 25 now. That’s not possible. So as I scale up...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But you said 2500 by end of the year.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: That’s six months.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Right. It’s six months. But it’ll be a gradual slope to 2500. I have enough inventory now for at least say 70 80 people. I add a bit more, I can get to 100. Now those 100 people are billing up front and then they get…

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And that accounts for all the different size variations?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Mm. So they’re clustered.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And different styles?

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: They’re all clustered.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So there’s two things that are always true about starting a business. It always costs more and it always takes longer And I’ve never met an entrepreneur that says, you know what my problem is? I just raised too much money. It doesn’t usually work that way.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Got it.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So here’s the thing. I’m going to pass, but this is what I have to say. I really like you and I love your ambitions. I have rarely seen an entrepreneur come in and say on 25 cents I can get to the moon. And you’re doing it. And good on you. And I love it. umm I’m going to pass But I really like you and I think you’re fixing an interesting problem.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Thank you. Appreciate it

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I think it’s a very smart idea. I see the value to consumers. I can really see people using it. I have concerns about the operations and logistical part of it.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I think umm the inventory issue is… is capital intensive You’re going to have to spend a lot of money for inventory. And right now marketing hasn’t been tested really.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Let me say this. I see your hesitation. Maybe we could take this offline. Because I measure tack time on jet blades. One thing I’m sure about is operations. So maybe I can take this offline and walk you through it.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Fair enough if you can convince me of the operational piece I may come in as an angel investor. But I’m going to pass for now.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Sure. No, I would love to take the chance. Appreciate it. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I feel if this were San Francisco, this would be a 500 on 3 kind of deal. Mostly because... Its’ weird. I suspect you’ll get more out of $100,000 than the average entrepreneur that we meet. It’s just weird for me as an investor, I’m fighting my natural desire to recoil when I feel like somebody is asking for too little money.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I think your capital raise doesn’t match your ambition.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: To me a $1 million cap is for someone who has nothing. Who hasn’t figured out anything. There’s serious questions about the model, there’s serious questions... I think this is a business that I think deserves half a million dollars so that you can expand, begin to test the marketing, prove that the operation scales and that it’s manageable at thousands of customers, and then I think you’ll be really well set up.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Um. So ah... You are unusual because you are coming with here with such a depth of knowledge, and I think your McKinsey background definitely shined bright here for all of us. And I liked the way that you’ve addressed all of our issues. I, I do feel that you need to raise more.

turns.speaker: Rahul
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I do think that this is doing you a disservice. Because $100,000 in our world Doesn’t even make sense. Like $100 can’t buy you a cup of coffee. Right. And so...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Actually it can.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay. Good. Thank you, Phil. All right.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So I’m very sad to say that I’m passing because I think you have such grit and potential And I want to see where this goes. I really do want to see where this goes.
